title: 10DLC for Colleges and Universities: 2026 Registration Guide
summary: How colleges register for A2P 10DLC: who owns the brand, how departments and OPMs map to campaigns, RFI opt-in language, rejections, fees and timelines.
body_markdown:
Colleges and universities need A2P 10DLC registration to text students from standard 10-digit phone numbers. The institution's legal entity registers once as the brand, with its exact legal name and EIN. Each type of messaging, such as admissions follow-up or financial aid reminders, is then registered as a campaign under that brand, using the standard Higher Education use case, because the K-12 special use case excludes post-secondary schools.


The mechanics of brands, campaigns and The Campaign Registry (TCR) are the same in every industry, and our[general A2P 10DLC guide](https://www.apten.ai/blog/a2p-dlc-compliance-2026) covers them. This guide is about what's specific to higher ed. A university is one legal entity with a dozen offices that text students, some through a CRM, some through a texting vendor, and some through an online program manager (OPM) that runs enrollment for a whole online division. Each setup changes who registers what.


Twilio has blocked all unregistered 10DLC messages to US numbers since September 1, 2023, and it still bills for the blocked messages. A rejected campaign in the weeks before a start date means admissions can't text new RFIs at all.


## Do colleges and universities need 10DLC registration?


Yes, if you send texts from a 10-digit number through any software. That covers your CRM's texting module, a two-way texting platform, an AI enrollment agent, and the softphone your advisors use. Carriers count all of it as application-to-person (A2P) traffic, even when a person types each message. Liaison's TargetX help center puts it bluntly for schools on Twilio: carriers "consider all messages that originate from Twilio to be A2P," so even one-to-one advisor texts need a registered campaign.


Drexel's IT office shows how this looks inside a university. Its 10DLC notice lists two allowed uses for texting on the university phone service: individual casual communication, and "department business units for communication with students, patients and other university partners." Every department that texts students needs registration, not just admissions.


Toll-free numbers and short codes go through their own verification instead. Neither gets you out of consent rules, which our[2026 guide to TCPA, FCC and state laws](https://www.apten.ai/blog/ai-compliance-guide-2026-tcpa-fcc-state-laws) covers.


## Who registers the 10DLC brand: the university or the vendor?


The brand is the legal entity sending the messages, and for a college that's the institution. Twilio's ISV documentation defines a brand as "the sender of a messaging use case, such as your customer's company." The brand record needs:


-


**The exact legal name tied to your EIN.** Twilio says to use the "exact legal business name as registered with the EIN." For many public universities that's something like "Board of Regents of..." or "Trustees of...", not the name on your website. A mismatch here is a common reason brands fail.


-


**The right entity type.** Twilio's fields include a government company type with a GOVERNMENT industry, and a non-profit type with a NOT_FOR_PROFIT industry. Public institutions usually register as government and private nonprofits as nonprofit. For-profit career colleges register as private or public companies.


-


**A working website related to the legal name.** Parked domains, login walls and redirects to an unrelated brand fail review.


-


**An institutional contact email.** Twilio says free email accounts and distribution-list addresses cause brand failure.


University systems need one more decision. If each campus has its own EIN, each campus is its own brand. If the system shares one EIN, campuses register under it, and T-Mobile's daily cap is tracked at the EIN level, so they share it. Twilio warns that newly issued EINs can take 30 to 90 days to show up in the databases that validate them, so a newly formed online entity should register early.


### When an OPM or vendor sends texts on the school's behalf


This is where higher ed differs most from other industries. An OPM, a texting vendor or an AI agent provider often holds the messaging account and does the registration. That's fine, but they should register *your institution* as the brand, using your legal details.


Twilio's ISV guide tells vendors to create a secondary customer profile and brand for each customer, and to "use that customer's details rather than your own ISV's details." A vendor that puts your admissions texts under its own brand, or under one shared campaign for all its schools, is registering the traffic wrong. Carriers can filter or suspend it.


Ask any OPM or vendor these questions before they file:


-


Is the brand registered under our legal name and EIN, or yours?


-


Who can see the registration status and the vetting score?


-


If we end the contract, what happens to the campaign and the phone numbers? Can the numbers be ported to us or to a new provider?


-


Whose name do the messages carry, and does our RFI consent language name that sender?


That last question matters for OPMs that run lead generation. The FCC's one-to-one consent rule was vacated by the Eleventh Circuit in January 2025, so it no longer applies. Consent still has to cover the institution actually texting the student. A form that says "partner schools may contact you" is weak ground for a university's texts, both legally and in carrier review.


## How should university departments map to 10DLC campaigns?


A campaign describes one kind of messaging: what you send, how people opt in, and sample messages. Departments with different content and opt-in flows should usually be separate campaigns. One vague campaign mixing admissions marketing and registrar alerts invites rejection.


Office Typical messages Likely use case Where opt-in happens


Admissions / enrollment RFI follow-up, program questions, info session invites, application reminders Higher Education RFI form, application, event sign-up


Financial aid FAFSA and verification reminders, award notices Higher Education Application or student portal


Registrar Registration windows, deadlines, holds Higher Education or Account Notification Student portal


Student success / advising Advisor check-ins, appointment reminders Higher Education Portal or advising sign-up


Campus safety Emergency alerts Often a dedicated alert platform; confirm with your provider Alert system enrollment


Advancement / alumni Event invites, giving appeals Confirm with your provider; fundraising content is reviewed closely Alumni forms, event sign-up


There's a catch that departments often miss. T-Mobile's daily cap applies per brand, not per campaign. Bandwidth's documentation says the cap covers "SMS, MMS, and all campaigns under a brand (per EIN)." If admissions sends a large re-engagement blast to aged inquiries, it draws from the same daily pool as the financial aid office's verification reminders. Coordinate big sends across offices, or you can hit the cap mid-day. Messages over the cap are rejected until it resets at midnight Pacific. If you're planning that kind of outreach, our guide to[re-engaging aged student inquiries](https://www.apten.ai/blog/re-engage-aged-student-inquiries) covers pacing.


## Does higher ed qualify for the K-12 special use case?


No. TCR's K-12 Education use case, available since November 2021, is a special use case with carrier post-approval. Twilio's use case reference describes it as "Campaigns created for messaging platforms that support schools from grades K-12 and distance learning centers. This is not for Post-Secondary schools." Twilio's changelog says K-12 campaigns get higher message limits and lower carrier fees, which is why colleges ask about it.


Colleges use the standard **Higher Education** use case, "for campaigns created on behalf of Colleges or Universities," which needs no carrier post-approval and bills at the standard monthly rate.


## What sample messages and opt-in language work for RFI forms?


Carriers compare three things: your opt-in language, the message flow you describe in the campaign, and the messages you actually send. All three need to match. Liaison's guidance for schools says samples should "include your institution name and show STOP and HELP keywords." Twilio's registration fields require at least two and at most five sample messages, each identifying the brand.


### RFI form checkbox


Keep the box unchecked by default and put the language next to it, not in a linked policy:


> \[ \] Yes, I agree to receive text messages from Example University about my inquiry, programs, application and enrollment, including automated messages, at the mobile number provided. Message frequency varies. Message and data rates may apply. Reply STOP to opt out or HELP for help. Consent is not required to apply or enroll. See our Privacy Policy and Terms.


Replace "Example University" with the name students know. If an OPM operates the program, the form should still name the institution sending the texts. The privacy policy link must be public. Twilio rejects policies behind a login, and requires the policy to say mobile numbers won't be shared.


### Campaign description and message flow


Vague descriptions get rejected. A specific one looks like this:


> Example University's admissions office texts prospective students who requested information about a degree program. Messages answer program questions, share info session times, remind students about application steps, and offer calls with an admissions advisor.


The message flow should name every place a student opts in, with a public URL for each. If the opt-in sits behind your application portal login, Liaison's guidance is to provide a screenshot URL so reviewers can see it.


### Sample messages


-


"Hi Jordan, it's Example University admissions. Thanks for asking about the online BSN. Want me to send the next start dates and prerequisites? Reply STOP to opt out."


-


"Example University: Your info session for the MBA program is tomorrow at 6pm ET. Join here: \[link\]. Reply HELP for help, STOP to opt out."


-


"Hi Jordan, Example University here. Your application is missing one transcript. Want to talk it through with an advisor today? Reply STOP to opt out."


Send a confirmation text after opt-in. CTIA's Messaging Principles call for one that names the program, gives customer care contact or HELP instructions, explains how to opt out, and discloses that messages are recurring and how often they come.


If an AI agent writes the replies, register samples that show conversational follow-up, not only one-way reminders, and keep the agent within what the campaign describes. What student data the agent can see is a separate question, covered in[FERPA and AI agents for prospective students](https://www.apten.ai/blog/ferpa-ai-agents-prospective-students) .


## Why do school 10DLC registrations get rejected?


College rejections tend to come from the same short list:


1.


**Legal name doesn't match the EIN.** The brand says "Example University Online" and the IRS record says "Board of Trustees of Example University."


2.


**The website doesn't connect to the brand.** An OPM-run microsite on its own domain, with no clear tie to the university's legal name, gives reviewers nothing to verify.


3.


**The opt-in can't be seen.** The consent language sits inside a portal with no screenshot, or the RFI form has no texting disclosure at all.


4.


**Privacy policy problems.** It's behind a login, it's a PDF on another domain, or it doesn't say mobile numbers won't be shared.


5.


**A use case that doesn't fit the content.** Marketing-style program promotion registered as Account Notification, or a single "general university messaging" campaign covering everything.


6.


**Samples without the school's name or opt-out language.**


7.


**Reused contact details.** Twilio says a contact mobile number can appear on no more than three brand registrations across TCR, and an email or street address on no more than ten. A central IT number used for every department's registration, or by several vendors, can hit that limit.


8.


**A personal or shared inbox as the brand contact.**


Each rejection costs time, and sometimes money. Twilio charges $11 to appeal a Standard brand vetting rejection, and campaign vetting fees aren't refunded.


## How long does 10DLC registration take, and what does it cost?


Here's what Twilio and TCR list as of October 2026. Other providers pass through similar registry fees but price carrier surcharges differently.


Fee Amount When


Brand registration with TCR $4.50 One time per brand


Standard brand vetting $41.50 One time, during Standard brand registration


Brand vetting appeal $11 Per request, only after a Standard vetting rejection


Campaign vetting (Twilio) $15 Per campaign submission, non-refundable


Monthly campaign fee, Higher Education $10 Per campaign per month (TCR standard rate)


Monthly campaign fee, Low Volume Mixed $1.50 Per campaign per month


Carrier per-message surcharges Fractions of a cent per segment Varies by carrier and provider. Check your provider's current rate sheet


A university with four department campaigns on Twilio pays about $46 once for the brand, $60 in campaign vetting, and $40 a month in campaign fees, before carrier surcharges and per-message pricing.


Timelines are less predictable. Brand registration is usually the quick step if the legal name and EIN match. Campaign vetting is manual. Twilio estimates campaign approval at under a week but says it can't give an exact timeline, because carriers and outside vetting partners are involved. AWS warns that its 10DLC campaign reviews take at least 4 to 6 weeks. Plan for a month, and assume one round of rejection and resubmission. If your fall or January start is the deadline, file in the summer or early fall.


## What throughput will a registered college get?


Throughput depends on your brand's vetting score, and unvetted brands start in the lowest tier.


Vetting score T-Mobile daily cap (per brand) AT&T SMS per minute (per campaign)


75 to 100 200,000 4,500


50 to 74 40,000 2,400


25 to 49 10,000 240


1 to 24 or unvetted 2,000 240


Figures are from Telnyx and Bandwidth's published limits as of October 2026. Low Volume Mixed campaigns get 75 messages per minute on AT&T. A 2,000-a-day T-Mobile cap shared across every department is tight for an admissions office working thousands of RFIs a week, which is the practical argument for paying for vetting.


## A 10DLC checklist for colleges and universities


1.


Pull the exact legal name, EIN and entity type from your business office, and confirm the system-versus-campus structure.


2.


Inventory every office and vendor that texts students, including OPMs, CRMs, advisor softphones and AI agents. Make each one file under your brand.


3.


Write one campaign per type of messaging, with a specific description, a public opt-in URL and two to five branded samples.


4.


Update RFI forms and applications with texting consent that names the institution and links to a public privacy policy.


5.


Set up a confirmation message, STOP and HELP handling, and a way for opt-outs to reach your CRM.


6.


Agree on a shared send calendar so one office's blast doesn't use up the brand's daily T-Mobile cap.


7.


File at least a month before your next inquiry peak.


This isn't legal advice. Review consent language and texting programs with your institution's counsel.

Apten is a multichannel AI enrollment agent. It texts, calls, emails and chats with prospective students, with one memory across every channel. Because texting is usually the first touch on a new RFI, registration has to be done before the agent can work.

## The bottom line


For a college, 10DLC is mostly an ownership question. Register the institution as the brand under its real legal name, give each office a campaign, make every vendor and OPM file under your brand, and name your school in the RFI consent language. Do that and the registry steps are routine. Skip it and you'll find out when admissions texts start failing a week before the start date.
